summary: FinanceCorpusBench v0.2 is an open golden-evaluation benchmark for financial-domain LLM corpus governance, archived for citation with a persistent DOI. It contains 120 golden samples in four JSONL subsets covering financial QA, Text-to-SQL, compliance judgment, and evaluator conformance testing. Metric naming aligns with YD/T 6486-2025; compliance design cross-references GB/T 45654-2025 and the JR/T financial standards. summary: Reference front approximations for 105 constrained multi-objective benchmark problems: the eight problems of the CRE suite, 49 of the 50 problems of the real-world constrained suite of the CEC 2021 competition (RCM01–RCM50 without RCM17) and 48 constrained problems of the human-powered aircraft design benchmark HPA. For each problem, the record gives its reference front, a sample of up to 100 points of the front with their decision variables, the union of all the feasible non-dominated solutions found, a sample of random solutions and a row of metadata: dimensions, ideal and nadir points, normalized hypervolume, stability across seeds, feasible rate, constraint-violation normalization and constraint descriptors. The fronts were computed with VAMOS, and independent implementations of the reference code of each suite re-evaluate every sample point. README.md describes every file; the folders are zip archives that unpack into the files listed in MANIFEST.sha256.
title: CRE, RCM and HPA reference fronts: Pareto front approximations, Pareto set samples and indicator metadata

summary: This dataset accompanies the revised article “Counting Disruption: Military Reporting and the Measurement of Weakening in Opération ‘Courroie’, Algeria, 1959,” submitted to War in History . The package contains the complete eleven-unit sector-level analytical dataset used in the revised study, together with the coding rules, reproducibility files, analytical workbook, scripts, and figure-generation materials. The primary attrition measure is the recorded neutralisation total for each French reporting sector. Subsequent Activity (SA) is a composite visibility measure based on engagements, mine incidents, sabotage acts, and documented insurgent presence during the ninety-day post-operational period. The eleven reporting units constitute the complete Courroie sectoral reporting grid used in the analysis. The dataset is designed to reproduce the descriptive comparison reported in the article, including Pearson and Spearman correlations and the sensitivity check excluding K543. It does not constitute a complete person-level transcription of all neutralisation records or a complete event-level census of all post-operational incidents. The revised analytical package does not use a Weighted Neutralisation Index (WNI) as an analytical measure. Rank remains relevant only as a historical feature of French reporting practices. The package is intended for transparent replication of the published sector-level analysis and for methodological scrutiny of how French military reporting converted recorded losses into claims about organisational weakening.
title: Opération "Courroie", Algeria, 1959: Revised Sector-Level Dataset and Reproducibility Package

summary: Abstract What is new. The individual tools here are known: Fr´echet bands, Vorob’ev gluing, toric selection, Picard–Lefschetz moves. What is new is one geometric landscape in which a decision maker’s information state is a point that moves as evidence arrives, and every change it un- dergoes is located, typed and given a consequence. The credal fibre shows what the data leave open; the walls of the mirror potential show where the description changes; each wall is classified as forced or computed. A collision of critical values is forced: the two hypotheses are orthogonal and the crossing is canonical, in every fibre dimension. A caustic forces its intersection number, but the side from which it was approached is a convention the data cannot fix. A Stokes event carries intersection numbers that must be computed. Rings of contexts show where gluing fails and by how much. The history of the state records what can be committed at once and what must wait. The landscape is mapped completely for 2 × 3 tables, at the level of critical values for 3 × 4, and by calibration for 3 × 3. It explains how an information state flows; whether it also anticipates decisions earlier than simpler records is an open, registered question. The geometry in brief. A conditioned state is a geometric object. The laws compatible with what has been observed form a polytope, the credal fibre. Its faces are cut out by the cells of the tables, and its vertices are certified by bases that come in dual pairs: the positive cells of a vertex form a spanning tree of the bipartite graph of the table (a graphic-matroid basis), and the zero cells form the complementary cographic basis, whose normals span the vertex cone. Conditioning maps the fibre onto a polytope of conditional laws, and the probability bands we report are coordinate projections of that polytope. Evidence acts on it by a projective map, an isometry of the Hilbert metric. Sampling noise is described differently: under regular sampling conditions it is asymptotically a Fisher–Rao confidence region, whose square-root image on the round sphere is approximately a spherical cap of radius of order m−1/2. Toric K¨ahler geometry supplies the selected law inside the fibre, its scales and its walls; the chamber complex of the margins supplies the stratification along which all of this changes. The note develops this picture and tests every computable claim against exact, pre-registered checks. A running example. A water authority must decide whether to keep seeding storms with silver iodide. It continues if q = P (above-normal rain | seeded, wet forecast) is at least a cost ratio θ. The records arrive in pieces: monthly flight counts, monthly rain categories, and later the 2 × 3 table of seeded and unseeded storms against above-normal, normal and below-normal rain. We follow this one synthetic data stream through the whole construction and back to the decision (Studies 83–90, held-out seeds, every check pre-registered and frozen with SHA-256). The data give a credal fibre and its probability bands; the margins give toric chambers and walls; the margins also set the mirror potential of the degree-six del Pezzo surface, whose thimbles form an exceptional collection in its Fukaya–Seidel category. The experiment is a carrier for a realistic decision problem, not a claim about seeding. 1 What the example verifies. Each layer is tested on held-out data: (i) credal walls lie on the chamber walls, while Stokes events are mutations; (ii) margin-order ties are collision walls where two orthogonal objects swap, confirmed at the Floer level on 10 of 12 brackets (the other two, one not audited and one with a non-minimal representative, stay in the record); (iii) a full twist of the potential acts as the Serre functor; (iv) the support region of a vector-valued hypothesis is cut out by Markov moves on the table; (v) poisoning that preserves the
title: Conditioned States as Toric K¨ahler Data A companion note to "Probability, Context and Differentiation: The Layers"

summary: This paper proves, in Lean 4 with Mathlib, what is forced about a system of spins that has a flip. A system is any finite set of states with a map of the states to themselves that is its own inverse, a weight the map keeps, and a count of up spins that the map sends to its complement. No lattice, no dimension, no range and no sign of the coupling is assumed. For every such system the partition function, as a polynomial in the activity $z$, is its own fold: its value at $1/z$ times $z^n$ is its value at $z$. Its zeros therefore come in folded pairs. The circle of unit modulus is the line of that fold: a point of the plane other than zero is kept by the map $z \mapsto 1/\bar z$ exactly when it is on the circle. For two spins the zeros are on the circle exactly when the coupling is inside its bound, and outside the bound every zero is real and off the circle. For three spins on a triangle the polynomial factors, and its zeros are on the circle inside the corresponding bound. In every such system any reading the flip reverses has total zero against the weight, so a finite system in no field has no net magnetisation. The file has 17 theorems, declares no axiom and leaves no proof open. That the zeros lie on the circle for every number of spins with ferromagnetic coupling is the theorem of Lee and Yang [2]; it is cited and is not proved here. Particle and Force Series, paper 2 of 14. Edition 1.0.0 (26 November 2026). This edition has not been put through an audit cycle. The full text and sources are also in the public Trisduction Git register (1000sapients/Trisduction).
title: The Ferromagnet as a New Mathematical Theorem: The Partition Function Is Its Own Fold for Every System of Spins with a Flip, the Circle Is the Line of That Fold, and the Zeros of Two and of Three Spins Lie on It Exactly Inside the Bound

summary: We resolve the open question of Bozóki and Csató (arXiv:2603.24274, Section 5, Example 5) affirmatively by constructing an explicit 4×4 rational pairwise comparison matrix with Perron eigenvalue 5 whose positive right eigenvector induces the strict ranking 1 ≻ 2 ≻ 3 ≻ 4 while the entrywise reciprocal of its positive left eigenvector induces the strictly opposite ranking 4 ≻ 3 ≻ 2 ≻ 1. We also characterize the full-reversal class via diagonal rescaling to constant-row-sum pairwise comparison matrices and formalize Saaty's n = 3 sharpness theorem in Lean 4.
title: Full Rank Reversal Between Right and Inverse Left Perron Eigenvectors for Four Alternatives (Resolution of Bozóki–Csató, arXiv:2603.24274)

summary: Evidence archive for: Mohammed, I.; Cho, H.; Shashidhar, N. Model Rollout Evasion: Quantifying and Predicting Evasion Exposure During Progressive Deployment of Machine Learning Detectors (manuscript submitted to Electronics, MDPI). Study summary Machine learning intrusion detectors are updated through progressive rollouts, during which two model revisions serve traffic at the same time. RolloutSecBench serves two frozen XGBoost revisions trained on UNSW-NB15 behind a weighted router on a single-node Kubernetes cluster and records the revision that served every request. Four rollout states (0%, 10%, 50% and 100% of traffic to the newer revision) are crossed with a non-adaptive attacker that submits each malicious sample once or five times, with five valid runs per condition. Although both revisions passed the same acceptance criteria, they disagreed on 149 of 38,263 malicious samples (0.389%). Resubmission increased evasion only while both revisions served, and within individual runs exposure followed the realized routing of the disagreement set rather than the configured weight. Version 1.1 adds the extension analyses of the revised article: duplicate-aware disagreement, alternative tests of the confirmatory decisions, a routing simulator validated on all 40 runs, 72 further revision pairs on UNSW-NB15 and CIC-IDS2017, live runs under session-affinity and content-keyed routing, offline attacker variants and a directional-disagreement gate. Contents rolloutsecbench-evidence-v1.tar.gz (confirmatory campaign; unchanged from version 1): Frozen model artifacts of both detector revisions and the preprocessor Pre-registration and analysis manifests of the confirmatory campaign Append-only run registry: 41 runs executed, 40 valid; the one invalid run was replaced by a pre-registered reserve Request-level client and router evidence for every run The analysis of record ( analysis_20261022T200702Z ), including the six files that supply the values and generated tables of the confirmatory campaign rolloutsecbench-evidence-ext-v1.1.tar.gz (extension analyses; new in version 1.1): Outputs of the extension analyses, with the values and tables of the article that they supply Raw client and router evidence of the 12 live routing-policy runs and 4 qualification runs, with their registry Data and provenance of the revised figures and tables In both archives, samples are identified by identifier only; no feature values of either dataset are included. Not included The UNSW-NB15 dataset, the corrected CIC-IDS2017 release and the split files derived from them are not redistributed. UNSW-NB15 is distributed by its authors (free for academic research; commercial use by agreement with the authors), and the corrected CIC-IDS2017 release by its providers. The released code recreates the UNSW-NB15 splits from the two official files and verifies them against Table S1 of the article. The plan of the extension analyses is not included; its SHA-256 and timestamp proof are listed in Table S4 of the article. Integrity rolloutsecbench-evidence-v1.tar.gz , SHA-256 17b61615728b68b27c689b48258a1b78a3d095f14f5fc11a0d8eca8e34dd12ca rolloutsecbench-evidence-ext-v1.1.tar.gz , SHA-256 67661fa3526340700ab936debad50492e4ebe736f66fbb0c312fc3ea09b40510 Every file is listed with its SHA-256 in the archive manifests ( ARCHIVE_MANIFEST.sha256 , EXTENSION_MANIFEST.sha256 ). The SHA-256 identities of the data, models, frozen predictions, router code and protocol, per-run checksums, run registry, analysis manifests, these archives and the code release are reported in Tables S1–S4 of the article. summary: Background. We propose subjecting specific cell populations to selective pressures analogous to reproductive competition observed among animals and other organisms, including mate harassment and sexual coercion. Classical oncology frequently confronts cancers with cytotoxic agents and maximal cell killing, imposing Darwinian selection that can ultimately contribute to the host’s demise; evolution itself has been identified as a proximate cause of death in most cancer patients (Enríquez-Navas et al., 2015). We hypothesize that exploiting existing cellular dependencies in replication-competent cells, in conjunction with their endogenous parasexual mechanisms, may drive those dependencies toward population-wide predominance. Through delivery by any suitable vector capable of inducing a pro-fusogenic state, the intervention may promote homotypic cell fusion and establish the reproductive pressures necessary to initiate the proposed extinctive vortices. Objective. The Induced Extinction Vortex (IEV) exploits endogenous reproductive mechanisms to drive local populations of replication-competent cells toward extinction through parasexual processes. Methods. The IEV is specified in three sequential phases: parasexualization, viable reproductive opportunity scarcity, and reversion. Each phase is defined by threshold conditions and explicit failure criteria. The proposal is method-agnostic; no particular delivery vehicle, parasexual driver, or receptor set is prescribed. Any implementation capable of instantiating the IEV as specified falls within the scope of this proposal. These predefined failure criteria will serve as benchmarks for subsequent research, mathematical modeling, and experimental assays. Supporting literature. Existing research documents spontaneous cancer-cell fusion and parasexual recombination, alongside demographic effects observed in natural populations, including mate limitation, reproductive interference, and inbreeding depression. Evolutionary oncology has also demonstrated that adaptive responses can be redirected into lethal liabilities. To our knowledge, however, no study has integrated these phenomena into a unified extinction strategy, particularly one directed toward populations composed predominantly of parasexual cells. Their convergence represents an open frontier in evolutionary oncology. Conclusions. The proposal hypothesizes that introducing genetic material capable of shifting a parasexual reproductive dependency toward population-wide predominance could establish both intraspecific and interspecific vulnerabilities. To our knowledge, existing research supports the individual components of this proposition, but their integration into a unified strategy has neither been documented nor experimentally evaluated.
title: Inducing Extinctive Vortices in Cell Populations

summary: Peng's Question 5.1 in Section 5.1, page 21 of arXiv:2606.14435v3 has a negative answer for compact Hausdorff systems: an open-map obstruction, combined with finite observation languages, yields a system with shadowing that has no zero-dimensional compact Hausdorff shadowing extension. The construction pulls an open surjection over a convergent sequence back to the binary full shift and adds a full-shift component. Marked finite graph languages force any putative extension to give an impossible open zero-dimensional resolution of that surjection. A countable tower and its natural extension give a homeomorphism with the same obstruction, even when the proposed extension is allowed to be noninvertible. Time is one-sided and includes zero.
title: An invertible counterexample to Peng's zero-dimensional shadowing-extension question

summary: Extracted data, screening decisions (model and blinded human calibration), search logs, analysis code (R and Python) and Supplementary Material for a rapid systematic review of how controlled trials of mindfulness-based interventions for depressive symptoms in Asian and ethnic minority adolescents report cultural adaptation, with a meta-analysis. Registered protocol and updates: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/5X38H. Version 2 (27 November 2026) accompanies manuscript draft 9 (after five rounds of pre-submission review). Principal estimate (post hoc): six randomised trials without data-integrity flags, g = 0.83 [0.41, 1.26]; registered primary estimate g = 1.16 [0.33, 1.99]. Full-text assessment of 85 disputed model exclusions, retrieval of unread eligible reports and independent human coding of adaptation are pending; worksheets are in calibration/. A language model (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) performed first-pass screening, extraction, coding and the analyses. The authors inspected its exclusions, full-text decisions and extracted values with its decisions visible; the only step reproduced independently by humans is a blinded calibration sample of 127 records, in which the authors agreed with the model at chance level. See README.md and Supplementary Table S17.
title: Data and code: Cultural adaptation in mindfulness-based interventions for depressive symptoms in Asian adolescents, a rapid systematic review of reporting and a meta-analysis

summary: Characterization of the Evolutionary Stages of Medical Technology Implementation: Seven Case Studies At the beginning of this century, many scientists predicted that Man would fly to the moon; none of them, however, predicted an even more amazing event - that we would be able to sit in our living rooms and watch that first moon walk.   Similarly, many technological advancements in medicine are easy to foresee, but predicting the technology that will really change our lives is nearly impossible.   In the last 5 years, technologies that apply to many fields of medicine have been introduced.   In medical school, there are now interactive CD-ROM'S and Internet-based references which add multimedia to the training of our new physicians.   Virtual Reality has been applied in simulating surgery for training purposes, and in providing alternative communication means for the disabled.   Telecommunication technologies allow additional surgeons to not only view, but participate via robotic arms in operations at distant sites.   New diagnostic tools that use highly accurate sensors for earlier detection of diseases are being tested for many health problems, and will soon be accessible to all.   Hand in hand with diagnostic testing is genetic mapping and testing which is making it possible for physicians to better understand the causes of many diseases.   All of these technologies have the potential to benefit many people, but not all from even this short list will be widely implemented.   For most of the years since the inception of the American health care system, the medical profession and the hospital field selected technology based upon the criteria:   more, bigger, and faster.   The focus of concern about technology began to change about twenty years ago.   In this age of cost-based reimbursement, physicians have advocated investment in technologies which provide qualitative improvements in patient diagnostics and therapeutics.   While this strategy has generally raised the level of care and quality of life of patients, it also led to a medical arms race between institutions.     The public mood has also changed significantly.   Throughout the 1970's, concern centered on ethical and humanitarian issues..   Means were sought to limit the unbridled use of life-extending technologies when there was little or no prospect of reasonable recovery.   The right-to-die movement and the living will legislation were manifestations of this mood.   Quite a different dilemma was posed by the emergence of renal dialysis, a technology that was usually successful in saving lives and that returned many patients to a reasonable quality of life for several years.   The problem was cost because it emerged that patients who could benefit from this treatment were sometimes denied it because insurers could not or would not afford it.   At the same time, health care costs as a whole were outstripping inflation and the cry went up that technology was the culprit.   The 1980's were therefore dominated by attempts to control technology in order to cut costs - not much was heard about making the best use of technology.     Now the emphasis has changed again - not because the problem of cost has been solved but because it has become so serious that the whole question of health care delivery is being reviewed.   In the broader scope of health policy, one crucial issue is seen to be technology assessment .   This assessment includes determination of relative benefits of different methods, as well as their hidden, non-financial costs.   This arose with the realization that US health care may need to be rationed.   For this rationing to be rational, there is a need to know not so much what different treatments cost, but whether they work.     Perhaps the solution to the rationing issue lies in an examination of medical e
title: Characterization of the Evolutionary Stages of Medical Technology Implementation: Seven Case Studies

summary: An agent that invents a useful representation should be able to use it to investigate a later phenomenon. We introduce COMPDISC, a sequential four-stage integer-cascade benchmark in which a frozen language model authors executable distinctions and laws, selects measurements that test its competing predictions, and carries the resulting program into the next stage. In the locked v4 evaluation on a frozen 27B Qwen service ( qwen38-27b-frozen ; 263 audited calls), the model completed all four stages on all three mechanisms (CD31, CD32, CD33), scoring 32/32 and 48/48 on the first two held-out panels of each mechanism. Across nine Stage-3 pairs with three measurements per arm, adaptive inquiry achieved 485/576 (84.20%) versus 436/576 (75.69%) for uniform random querying (+8.51 percentage points; 5 wins, 3 ties, 1 loss), using 70 versus 19 Stage-3 model calls. Holding the fitted Stage-3 law fixed and substituting either earlier representation reduced accuracy by 75.39 and 72.66 percentage points across the eight retained trajectories with an adopted law. All 29 admitted initial hypotheses conflicted with accumulated observations (0/29 surviving); seven trajectories deployed a law generated during mid-probe refresh and one synthesized an exact fitting law at final commitment (64/64). This v1 release includes the preprint PDF and a sanitized, portable zero-model-call offline verification archive ( compdisc_v4_verification_bundle.zip ) containing the frozen harness code, task specifications, all 263 request/response receipts, and standalone verifier ( verify_release_offline.py ). Licensing: The preprint PDF, task specifications, receipts, and documentation ( *.pdf , *.json , *.md ) are licensed under CC BY 4.0. Python source code files ( *.py ) inside compdisc_v4_verification_bundle.zip are licensed under the MIT License (see LICENSE inside the archive).
title: Executable Representations for Cumulative Discovery: A Closed-Loop Benchmark for Frozen Language Models

summary: This replication package reconstructs the numerical results in “How flood forecast revisions affect substation protection and expected load shed.” The analysis measures how far flood-scenario probabilities must move before another substation protection plan becomes preferable, and how much expected operating loss can be avoided by changing plans. The Imelda study enumerates feasible deployments. The Harvey study evaluates archived alternatives and reviews full-investment solutions at selected, fixed forecasts. The archive contains the model inputs, Python scripts, reference CSV files, plotting routines, scenario weights, archived solver records and a replication guide. The default workflow runs offline after dependency installation, uses SciPy/HiGHS to recompute dispatch, checks the published values in Tables 1–4, and regenerates Figures 1–4. Eight archived Gurobi runs support the Harvey fixed-forecast results. A separate optional driver can launch new full-space searches with a suitable Gurobi license.
title: Replication package for "How flood forecast revisions affect substation protection and expected load shed"

summary: Supplementary data for "NWNet: orthology inference by small-world sparsification of all-against-all comparison" This archive contains the genome lists, sampling scripts and benchmark results used to prepare and evaluate the benchmarks in the NWNet manuscript (Lu, Zuo & Zhi). Contents ecoli/  —  Escherichia coli  genome acquisition and sampling: the 12,308 non-redundant, quality-filtered genome accessions, the 1,000-genome ANI-stratified sample, the 100–500 genome benchmark subsets, the fastANI results, and the sampling scripts. qfo/  — Quest for Orthologs 2022 benchmark: the local reference-phylogeny scoring scripts and the per-configuration SwissTree and TreeFam-A TPR/PPV scores for the nine evaluated configurations. Data sources The 404,453  E. coli  genomes were downloaded from the NCBI Assembly database on 17 June 2026. The QfO 2022 reference data are available from OpenEBench ( https://openebench.bsc.es ); the 78 species proteomes (988,778 proteins) are available from UniProt. Neither is re-packaged here.
